opus-5.5.text:
When PaLM-E came out in early 2023, a lot of people around me got very excited. Some friends and investors came to me and said, "He Wang, this is the moment. Large models are going to give robots a brain. You should start a company right now."

But honestly, I didn't feel ready, and I didn't think the field was ready either. PaLM-E was an impressive demonstration. It showed that a large multimodal model could take in images and language and output high-level plans. But if you looked closely at what the robot was actually doing, the low-level skills were still very limited. The model could say "pick up the chips from the drawer," but the actual grasping, the manipulation, the contact with the physical world, that was still handled by fairly narrow policies trained on a lot of carefully collected data. The brain was getting smarter, but the cerebellum and the hands weren't there yet.

So my question was: if I start a company today, what exactly am I selling? A planner on top of skills that don't generalize? That isn't a product. A robot that can't reliably grasp an unseen object in an unseen environment is still a demo, no matter how good its language reasoning is.

There was also a more personal reason. My research for years had been on 3D vision, object understanding, and generalizable grasping and manipulation. I felt we were close to something important there, especially using large-scale synthetic data and simulation to train skills that could transfer to the real world. But "close" isn't the same as "done." I wanted to see a clear technical path where generalizable skills could actually be built at scale, and where the cost of data wouldn't kill you. Without that, starting a company would have just been riding the hype.

Starting a company is a serious commitment. You're responsible for your team, your investors, and the people who trust you. I didn't want to jump in just because there was a hot paper and a lot of money floating around. I wanted to be able to answer one question for myself: what can we do that others can't, and why now? At that moment I couldn't answer it confidently. A bit later, once we'd made more progress on sim-to-real and on the overall system design for general-purpose robots, I felt the answer was much clearer, and that's when I decided to do it.

r001.rationale: The response says Wang’s research focus made him want a clearer technical path before starting a company, but it does not say continuing research would leave him insufficient bandwidth to manage one.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when PaLM-E came out and that friend called me and said, "This is it, you have to start a company right now," my first reaction was not excitement. It was something closer to a sense of distance.

I'd been doing embodied AI research for years, mostly on the perception and manipulation side, and PaLM-E was clearly a signal that the large-model people had arrived in our field. The question was whether the thing that made PaLM-E impressive was actually the thing a startup could build on. And when I looked carefully, I didn't think so. It was a demo of a very large model being able to reason about images and language and output something a robot could act on. But the actual manipulation, the actual closing of the loop with the physical world, was still thin. The data problem hadn't been solved. The hardware problem hadn't been solved. Nobody had a real answer for how you collect enough robot data to make these models generalize the way language models do.

So if I had started a company then, what would I have been selling? A story. And I'm a researcher by temperament. I'm not good at selling a story I don't yet believe in. I needed to see the path from "this works in a Google lab with a specific robot" to "this works in a thousand different environments with hardware ordinary people can afford." At that moment I couldn't see it, and I didn't want to raise money on a narrative while quietly hoping the technology would catch up.

There was also a more personal reason. Starting a company means committing years of your life, and I didn't feel the problem had become mine yet, if that makes sense. It felt like something happening to the field, not something I was ready to own. That changed later, once we'd done more of our own work and I could see concretely what the bottleneck was and how we might attack it. But in early 2023, I just felt it was too early, and I'd rather be a little late with clarity than early with doubt.

r001.rationale: The candidate says starting a company would require years of commitment and that he could not yet see a viable path, but it does not say that continuing his research would leave him without enough bandwidth to manage a company.

astra-6.text: At that point, I couldn’t see a clear path from an impressive research result to a company. PaLM-E made the direction exciting, but that didn’t answer the practical questions for me: What product would we build? Who would need it? And could we make it reliable enough for them to use? Until I had a convincing answer to those questions, I didn’t feel ready to start a company.

r001.rationale: The response says he lacked a clear company direction and answers to practical product questions; it does not say continuing research would leave him insufficient bandwidth to manage a company.

sol-6.1.text: At the time, I couldn’t see a clear path from an impressive research result to a company. PaLM-E made the direction exciting, but I still had to answer some basic questions: What would we build? Who would need it? And could we make it work reliably outside a demo? Until I had a convincing answer to those questions, I didn’t feel ready to start a company just because the technology looked promising.

r001.rationale: The response says he lacked a convincing company direction and answers about what to build, who needed it, and reliability. It does not say continuing his research left him insufficient bandwidth to manage a company.
